task.title: Named strings
task.shortdesc: Named strings let a stylesheet save content from elements as a value and retrieve that value elsewhere. They are intended for paged content such as running headers and footers.

context.p: Before writing a rule, inspect your XML and find the element whose text or attribute you want to reuse. A CSS rule has a selector followed by declarations inside braces. The selector chooses which XML elements the declarations apply to. In these examples, a name such as title is a type selector: it matches elements with that name. It has no special meaning to CSSMedia. Replace example names such as title, group, and item with names that actually occur in your XML. Each declaration sets a property using property: value; syntax. See Selectors overview for other ways to choose elements.

info.p: CSS Content 3 §2.7.1, The string-set property; CSS GCPM 3 §1.1.1.1, The content() function.

CSS Content 3 specifies none or one or more comma-separated pairs, each containing a <custom-ident> followed by one or more strings. CSSMedia’s parser also accepts a <content-list> after each name. That broader form is a CSSMedia parser extension, not the specified value grammar. The initial value is none , which assigns no named strings.
The examples below use the parser extension so you can see its accepted syntax. CSSMedia currently validates string-set but does not save named strings or resolve the string() function.

Here, h1 is the selector, string-set is the property, and the text after the colon is its value. chapter-title is a name you choose for the saved value. It does not need to occur in the XML. content(text) takes the text from each selected element. Use the actual element name from your XML instead of h1 if it is different. A later matching element can replace the saved value with its own text. One declaration can save multiple values:
The <custom-ident> is an author-defined identifier. It cannot be a CSS-wide keyword or none.
The content is one or more items. The <content-list> grammar allows these forms:

ul.li: counter(<counter-name>, <counter-style>?) contributes the formatted value of the innermost counter with that name on the element.
counters(<counter-name>, <string>, <counter-style>?) contributes the formatted values of every in-scope counter with that name, from outermost to innermost, joining them with the required string.
content() reads text from the element or one of its generated parts.
attr(<attr-name> <syntax>?, <fallback>?) contributes an attribute value. The optional syntax controls how that value is parsed; the fallback is used when the attribute is missing or cannot be parsed.

info.p: CSS Lists 3 §4.3, Nested Counters and Scope; CSS Lists 3 §4.7, Outputting Counters; CSS Counter Styles 3, Counter styles.

Counters are values maintained by CSS. Use counter-reset, counter-increment, or counter-set to create or change them. A counter name is a <custom-ident> and cannot be none or a CSS-wide keyword. To include a counter value in generated content, use counter() or counters().

A reset of a counter with the same name inside an existing counter’s scope creates a nested counter. This lets repeated structures use one counter name at every depth. On an element inside those scopes:

ul.li: counter(name) returns only the innermost counter named name.
counters(name, separator) returns all in-scope counters named name, ordered outermost first and innermost last. separator is a CSS string inserted between the formatted values.

info.p: In the sample XML below, a group can contain item elements and another nested group. These names are examples. If your XML uses different element names, change the selectors to match them. The group rule starts an item counter at zero for each group. The item rule increases that counter by one for each item. The item::before rule adds generated text before each item’s own text. Its content value calls both counter functions: counter(item) shows only the current, innermost number; counters(item, ".") shows the number at each nesting level, separated by a period.

The first two items display 1 (1) and 2 (2). The nested items display 1 (2.1) and 2 (2.2). In each function, the optional <counter-style> selects how each number is represented. If omitted, the style is decimal. For example, counters(item, ".", upper-roman) joins values formatted as uppercase Roman numerals. A <counter-style> can be the name of a predefined or author-defined @counter-style, or a symbols() function.
If the named counter does not exist at the point of use, CSS first creates it with a value of 0. The counter functions return formatted text; they do not substitute the source element’s contents.
The content() function takes one optional keyword:

ul.li: text reads the element’s text, treating whitespace as if white-space: normal applied. This is the default when the argument is omitted.
before reads the text of the element’s ::before pseudo-element.
after reads the text of its ::after pseudo-element.
first-letter reads the first typographic letter, following the rules for ::first-letter.

info.p: CSS GCPM 3 §1.1.1.1, The content() function; CSS Values 5 §7.7, The attr() notation.

Use content(text) to save an element’s text from the XML tree, including text inside descendant elements, in document order. Whitespace is handled as if white-space: normal applied. Text generated by ::before or ::after is not part of this value. Use content(before) or content(after) to read the corresponding pseudo-element’s generated text instead.

Use attr(name) to save an attribute from the element matched by the rule. Without a syntax, CSS treats the attribute’s literal value as a string. If the attribute is missing, the value is an empty string unless you provide a fallback. A fallback can supply text for missing or unparseable attribute values.

This sample XML has a title element, a code attribute, and an em child element. These names are examples; use the names and attributes present in your own XML. A CSS selector containing just title matches each title element. A selector such as title::before targets generated content before that element’s XML text.

Inside the title rule, the three comma-separated assignments save three values. title-text is the name chosen for the element’s text. title-prefix saves what the ::before rule generates. title-code saves the code attribute, or “No code” when that attribute is missing. attr(code) reads from the element selected by title, not a child or ancestor.

The @page rule applies settings to pages in the PDF. The nested @top-left and @top-right rules put content in the left and right positions of the top page margin. Their content declarations retrieve the saved values with string(name). The left margin displays “Chapter A-4”; the right margin displays “Install the package”. For a title without code, the left margin displays “Chapter No code”.

A named string’s value is assigned when the element’s content box is created, or would be created if display: none applies. The values can change as matching elements occur in the document. The layout process must retain these successive assignments because string() can request a value from a particular point on a page.

step.cmd: Retrieve a named string with string()

info.p: CSS GCPM 3 §1.1.2, The string() function; CSS Paged Media 3 §4.1, The @page rule; CSS Paged Media 3 §5.1, At-rules for page-margin boxes.

Use string(<custom-ident>, <mode>?) in a content value to retrieve a named string. The first argument is the name you wrote in string-set. The optional second argument selects which assignment to use on the page. For example, chapter-title below must match the name after string-set in the earlier example, or the name you used in your own stylesheet.
The mode accepts these four keywords:

ul.li: first selects the first assignment on the page. If there is no assignment there, it uses the value in effect at the end of the previous page. This is the default.
start selects the value in effect at the beginning of the page. If the named string has not yet been assigned, this value is empty.
last selects the value in effect at the end of the page.
first-except works like first, but returns an empty value on a page that contains an assignment to the named string.

info.p: The @page rule describes the page being produced. @top-center puts this content in the center of the top page margin.
